Throwing the seers to the earth, some Asuras trampled them underfoot, / like blazing fires, to their own destruction.
The vilest of Dānavas touched with their hands and palms the heads / of the wives of the sages, purified by sacred waters. // Then, knowing their own prosperity, they undertook the expedition, / having summoned from all sides the army deployed for the destruction of the world.
On an auspicious day, asterism, and victory-bringing muhūrta, / they sounded the war drums and performed the victory-bringing rites.

Bringing up the excellent elephants that were strong, noble, and fit to be armoured, / and properly worshipping the armour, the Asuras fastened it according to rule.
They bound engines filled with polished iron arrows on both sides of the seat, / and bamboo tubes filled with javelins, placed crosswise.
And the men appointed bound javelins, kaṇapas, spikes, / tridents, discuses, and battle-axes on the sides of the middle seat.
[They prepared] ready supreme weapons, and well-adorned quivers / filled with fragrant garments and sharp-pointed arrows.
On the neck-chains they placed iron goads ready for armor, shining like the crescent moon, / bright between the two frontal globes of the head.
And the elephant-riders bound upon the frontal globes of the elephants / an auspicious, fitted garland shaped like razor-pointed blades, made of gold.
And the ready Dānavas raised manifold, clearly visible victory banners / of the elephant division.

Armored foot-soldiers, their cuirasses fastened, wielding sharp swords, / were placed in front of them, followed by archers; / then other Daitya warriors, armored and clad in iron chain-mail, / their swords strapped on, mounted horses that had bathed and drunk.
Some then yoked chariots with well-trained, young horses, / bathed, decorated with auspicious marks, and born of the finest stock.
Some then mounted chariots adorned with gold, / furnished with weapons, bearing banners, and resounding with clusters of tinkling bells. / Having heard that the army was thus arranged, saluted by the army, / Sunda, that tiger among Dānavas, set forth, having performed auspicious rites.
Having mounted a divine chariot with fine pole, good yoke, and sound axle, made of gold, / adorned with diverse jewels and decorated with artistic figures of flowers, beasts, and birds, / yoked with exceedingly spirited horses swift as thought, / and beautified with banners and flags,

and quickly stationing the great Asura Mahiṣa, mad with strength, / as the rear-guard with a fourfold army behind him; / and having posted on both flanks Meghasvana and Mahāsvana, / two proud Dānavas, slayers of foes, with a mighty army;
in the center were Sunda, Nisunda, Maya, Śambhu, Khara, and Mura, / armored, mighty, and heroic, tearers of enemy ranks. / Fully prepared, those foremost of Dānavas set forth toward heaven / like the dissolution-clouds driven by the wind at the end of an aeon.
Knowing of their approach, Śatakratu, along with the dwellers of heaven, / fled and quickly went to Janasthāna. / Having ascended the peak of Meru, all together then, / those enemies of the gods encamped their army in the Nandana grove.
Then, having posted guards for the army on every side, / the Daitya lords took up spacious, divided quarters.

7.7.m:
Having removed the mail of battle-armor, the grooms tied up the horses separately, / their minds content, their bodies rubbed down, their thirst quenched, and their fatigue removed.
Then they brought fine garments and splendid variegated garlands, / and sweet fruits from the wish-fulfilling trees.
Their forms reddened by its pollen, some joyful Dānavas / entered the river Mandākinī and plucked golden lotuses.
Some soldiers brought heaps of mandāra flowers; / others fetched many sweet fruits.
Having spent one night there, the Dānavas, beating their drums, / proceeded with the same discipline, fully prepared, toward Amarāvatī.
Then, at the sound of the musical instruments, the trumpeting of the elephants, / and the lion-roars of the Daityas, Amarāvatī seemed to tremble.

Victorious is the enemy of the gods, the lion among Daitya lords, Sunda,
With hard, charming arms and a broad, stout chest, / the conqueror of Śatamakhu's city, with eyes lovely, wide, and long,
Roaring like a raincloud, striding like an elephant in rut!
Next to him is victorious [he] whose wide, charming eyes are red at the corners,
With the playful gait of a lion, unassailable in battles, / the conqueror of the best among the thirty [gods], the Dānava lord Nisunda,
Sounding like a beaten muraja drum, with thick, long, and massive arms!

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, entitled “The Entry into Amarāvatī,” in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having conquered heaven, the two valorous Daitya lords, / accompanied by the Daityas, went to the Vindhya, that lofty mountain.
Having honored the Daityas according to rule and dismissed them, the two brothers / then disported on the slopes of the Vindhya, on peaks with blossoming trees.
Then Brahmā, learning of the gods' defeat by the two Daityas, / reflected with single-minded focus on the means to slay them both.
Taking a particle from each jewel, he fashioned a lovely-looking woman / with desirable limbs and a sweet voice.
And the Grandfather gave her the name Tilottamā. / She shone then as the very ideal even for divine women.
Her face was utterly complete, her eyes surpassed the blue lotus, / her speech excelled the cry of the swan, her gait outshone an elephant in rut.
Seeing her, Lakṣmī covered her face bashfully with a lotus; / and with their forms, the deities of the garden were humbled by that fair-limbed woman.

Having created her, the Creator then spoke to the subduer of Pāka: / “Formerly, Madana was burned by Śambhu with the fire of his eye.
For his resurrection, let us all go to the side of the wielder of the Pināka; / having propitiated him, we shall act so that Madana may exist again.”
Then the enemies of the Asuras, together with Brahmā and with her, / went to the peak of the Vindhya mountain where the Blessed Lord Hara resides.
Not seeing Śarva there, those best of the gods meditated, / all reciting the Praṇava, with their minds surrendered to Śiva.
Then a liṅga arose in the midst of those heaven-dwellers, / compact and very cohesive, like an accumulation of fires. / Then from it a voice arose aloud, with clear syllables: / “That sinner, a thorn in the side of ascetics, was burned by me.

For your sake I will release him; he will accomplish your business. / And let this woman circumambulate me clockwise on all sides.”
Thus spoken to by the Great Lord, she circumambulated him clockwise, / placing on her head her folded hands, delicate as red lotuses.
She bowed then to the eastern face, and thereupon a face emerged, / three-eyed, with serene bimba-fruit lips, immeasurably brilliant and lovely. / Then a splendor, shining like the autumn sun, issued from the moon-like face / of the wielder of the Pināka, and swiftly entered that woman.
Then that lovely-looking woman bowed to the southern form; / thereupon the blazing face of the guru of the gods emerged from it,
Possessing the luster of a cloud languid with its burden of rain, with a dreadful sound, / gleaming with fierce fangs, its eyes blazing red at the corners.

By means of that splendor belonging to himself, which, having formerly burned Madana, was stored [in him], / the Lord of gods favored that best of women.
And Śiva spoke these words to all the gods there:

on the Vindhya mountain will be known as Maṇḍaleśvara.
Whoever performs circumambulation around this Maṇḍaleśvara,
by him the earth of seven islands has been circumambulated.
Indeed, granting boons, I shall always establish my presence here.

And Brahmā, whose vehicle is the lotus, gave her companions:
anger, arrogance, all the seasons, envy, and pride,
time, death, delusion, and despair, he of boundless splendour.
Then, having sent forth that Tilottamā, the deities—
all those gods indeed assembled themselves into a group:
“Who has arrived here today, and which one [is he]?” O bulls among gods.
Then, bowing again to the Supreme Lord who stood in their midst,
since he stood in the midst of the gods as they gathered together,
he then became known there as Piṇḍāreśvara.
A man, having beheld the Lord Piṇḍāreśvara with devotion,
freed from all misfortune, upon the dissolution of the body becomes a gaṇa.
Whatever liṅgas and four-faced shrines there are on earth—

Then all those deities, unwearied, having accomplished their purpose,
bowed to the Supreme Lord and departed to their own abodes.
And she, whose face and eye-corners were lovely, with firm, elevated breasts,
as if captivating the minds of the gods by her charms,
set forth toward the southern quarter where the two dānavas were.
Rambling at the delightful foothills of the Vindhya whose peaks were sung by birds,
the two daitya chiefs saw her standing there,
leaning against a blooming aśoka branch with frenzied bees,
wearing a variegated garment, with a jewelled girdle fastened,
singing sweetly, passionately, evenly, softly, and clear,
properly adorned with high, low, and very high notes,

“And I am Niśumbha!” the other boy said there then.
Then the Vindhya mountain, having approached those two boys of boundless splendour,
instructed his wife: “Protect these two children.”
Then both those sons of the dānava lords grew up there,
just like the moon and the ocean together at the end of the dark fortnight.
And those two tamers of foes, having then understood their birth from the dānavas,
performed very severe austerity, feeding on leaves, water, and wind.
Worshipped by them with austerity, the Lord came there and said:
“I am pleased with you two, my sons. What boon shall I give?”
The two heroes chose a boon: to be always unvanquished and invulnerable to death.
Hearing their prayer, the grandfather [Brahmā] replied:
"O sons, death is inevitable for both of you by one means or another.
O lords of Daityas, immortality exists nowhere apart from the gods."
When Brahmā had spoken thus, the two Dānavas chose a boon,

the two best of Dānavas roamed the delightful plateaus of the Vindhya.
Hearing of the attainment of the boon from the Grandfather by Śumbha and Niśumbha,
the Dānavas dwelling in the subterranean realm of Pātāla came forth rejoicing:
Śambhu, Maya, Ghana, Keśin, Naraka, Namuci, Druma,
and millions of other proud enemies of the gods who had survived slaughter.
All those Dānavas, assembled together, settled on the Vindhya plateau,
strewn with heaps of flowers from various trees, creepers, and shrubs,
armed with bows, girded with swords, adorned with colorful ornaments,
like rain-clouds in the sky bearing Indra's rainbows and lightning.
Then the Dānava Maya spoke there to the two foremost Dānavas:
"Formerly, the entire threefold world was enjoyed by your two fathers.
Why is it not taken back again by both of you now, O Daityas?
Having conquered in the vanguard of battle all the gods assembled together,
those very enemies of the gods who were allies of your two fathers,

"Our sovereignty indeed extends over the entire earth now, O Kaśyapa.
You ought to sacrifice to us in this sacrifice under all circumstances!"
Addressed thus by the Daityas, Kaśyapa the son of Marīci then
spoke these grave and meaningful words, as if smiling:
"Having made the threefold world your own and having conquered all the gods in battle,
then, O Daityas, you will be worthy to receive all the sacrificial shares!"
Spoken to thus by him at that time, those best of Daityas and Dānavas,
gathering all their army and performing the rites pertaining to war,
having observed traditional ceremonies at auspicious lunar hours, asterisms, and days,
those Daityas and Dānavas set out with chariots, elephants, and horses.
Properly arranging protection behind, ahead, and on both flanks,
prepared for battle, they marched, desiring to conquer the gods.

spoke these words with a smile, skilled in speech: / 'Know me to be a mortal woman who has made her home on this mountain.

7.7.m:
Hearing these words of the Goddess, Mūka, rejoicing in his heart, / hastened to behold Śumbha, the best of the Dānavas. // Approaching Śumbha with his eyes wide with joy, / he described, as it were through gestures, the sight of an unprecedented jewel [of a woman]:
Seeing him wide-eyed with wonder, Śumbha, whose long eyes were red, / then said to Mūka: 'Why are you pleased, O Dānava?'
Thus addressed by Śumbha, Mūka spoke these words: / 'Today on the mountain peak I have seen an unprecedented jewel of a woman!
No such beauty exists among humans, nor even among the gods, / nor among the Rakṣases, nor the Yakṣas, nor in the cities of the Gandharvas,
nor among the Nāgas, nor the Siddhas, nor in the dwellings of the Daitya kings, / has such an excellent woman ever been seen by me, O King! // "Who are you, whose are you, or why do you dwell on this mountain?"—

7.7.m:
Thus instructed by Śumbha, the Dānava rose quickly / and went to where that Goddess had previously been seen by him.
Seeing that Dānava standing before her with folded hands, / the Goddess then questioned Mūka: 'For what purpose have you come?'
Thus asked by Kauśikī, the Dānava Mūka replied: / 'Noble lady, I am Śumbha's messenger, come into your presence.
Then the Goddess, having smiled and looked kindly upon him, / spoke thus to the messenger who had arrived: 'What does he say, that lord of the Asuras?'
Questioned thus by the Goddess, Mūka with folded hands said: / 'Noble lady, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas, chooses you as his wife.
Of that lion among Dānavas, the conqueror of Śakra in battle, / become the foremost wife among all his wives, O deer-eyed lady!'
Thus addressed by him, the sovereign Goddess of the immortals laughed and said, / looking down at her own arms: 'Know me to be one whose bride-price is battle! // Only by defeating me in battle does that Daitya deserve to make me his wife. / Or, slain by me, let him become food for crows and jackals!'

7.7.m:
To the Goddess who had spoken thus, Mūka replied as if laughing: / 'What need have you for battle, O lovely lady, with the lord of the Dānavas and Daityas?
When he is enraged in battle, even the slayer of Vala and Vṛtra, / mounted on the shoulder of Airāvata, could not bear to gaze upon his face!'
Hearing those words of his, the Goddess, as if smiling, said: / 'All the lords of the Daityas are mere blades of grass to me in the forefront of battle! // Report [this] to Śumbha; go, you lowest of Dānavas!
Because you have arrived on a mission as an envoy, for that reason you are not slain by me.'

“I wooed that maiden for your sake, O best of Dānavas. / She said, ‘My bride-price is battle; having defeated me, you may take me.’
Moreover, O king, assuming pride, full of wonder, that woman said: / ‘The Daityas in battle are mere blades of grass to me.’
Then, having heard that speech of hers spoken by Mūka, / the best of Asuras could not endure it out of wrath, pride, and passion.
Then the lord of the Dānavas, rising up, went to the delightful assembly hall, / which had turrets of crystal pillars and archways of manifold jewels.
In it, upon a great, firm, golden throne covered with fine rugs, / the mighty-armed one sat down, as Varuṇa in [the city of] Sukhā.
After him, Niśumbha also sat down on an excellent seat, / his chest then illuminated by the rays of his jewel-encrusted armlets.
Following them, the Daityas and Dānavas of great might entered, / like clouds dark with water [entering] a delightful cave of the Himavat.
Then, when those kings of the Daityas and Dānavas were seated, / Śumbha, whose voice was like the rumbling of a cloud, uttered these words:

“All excellent women are perverse by their very nature. / Having once conciliated her, O king, you should take her.”
Having heard the words of Śambhu, Maya, the best of the Dānavas, / whose eyes were like freshly blossomed blue lotuses, spoke:
“What is her appearance, and what are her actions, O lord of the Asuras? / What are her companions, or what are her constant accoutrements?”
When Maya, the Daitya lord possessed of the prowess of a rutting elephant, had said this, / the ruler of the Daityas then urged Mūka standing at his side. / Whatever question Maya, best among the wise, asked there, / Mūka then began to recount it all:
“Always firmly stationed, having [three] distinct eyes, with terrible fangs and face, / eight-armed, dark as a raincloud, with a fine nose and pleasant voice;
by her side are always all kinds of weapons, / excellent armor, and wondrous ornaments.
Her body surpasses the sun, and her beauty surpasses the moon.” / Having thus spoken in the assembly of the Daityas, Mūka then fell silent.

Then all the best Daityas and Dānavas, impelled by Time, / consented to the words of the Daitya king.
Then, having addressed all the lions among the Daityas in the assembly at that time,
the conqueror of the lord of the thirty [gods], / whose pendant, pure, white, great necklace hung down,
flew up like a cloud in the rainy season, heavy with a burden of fresh water.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa […].
Sanatkumāra said:
Having beaten the kettle-drums and armored themselves, those sons of Diti and Dānavas / then equipped the chariots, elephants, and horses.
Then, having brought the elephants that had drunk water, / having given them incense and mouthfuls [of food] that increase their rut,
the Daityas equipped their girths, well-adorned neck-chains, / and goads made entirely of iron, decorated with gold and jewels.

The Dānavas, clad in iron mail and with swords girded on, / mounted horses that had bathed and drunk, were armored, and had tied tails. (7)
Certain car-warriors mounted chariots yoked with horses, / equipped with weapons and banners, well-joined, with excellent axles and poles. (8) / Then the two brothers Śumbha and Niśumbha, lords of the Dānavas, / those great Asuras maddened with strength, clad in armor, (9)
mounted two battle-ready, fully equipped chariots with prancing horses, / armed, bearing banners, and made of gold, each separately. (10) / Broad-chested, having had auspicious benedictions of victory pronounced over them, they set forth,
praised by Māgadhas, bards, and heralds marching in front. (11) / Then they began to march in ranks, sounding musical instruments, / toward that mountain around which the goddess Kauśikī dwelt. (12)

7.7.m:
Then that army of deities, adorned with banners and flags, / with sounding musical instruments, crowded with flashing scimitars, shone forth,
variegated like a line of cranes, accompanied by Indra's bow, possessing a great roar, / like a mass of rainclouds with lightning in the month of Bhādrapada.
Then that army of deities marched restraining [itself], facing the lord of the Daityas, / with swift speed, compressing, as it were, the ten directions. / Then the enemies of the gods saw the army approaching, with varied banners raised high, / inspiring terror, roaring loudly, like a towering mass of clouds at the dissolution of the world.
8.64.50. / Thus in the Skandapurāṇa, in the battle with Śumbha and Niśumbha, ends the sixty-fourth chapter, entitled "Description of the Army".

7.7.m:
Then those enraged deities struck the Daityas at the front / with diverse weapons, and they clashed with them in battle. / The Daityas, equipped with various weapons, then struck the goddesses in battle: / the foes of the immortals, [though] mighty heroes, [attacked] the women in combat.
Horsemen [fought] those on horses, and foot-soldiers foot-soldiers, / charioteers those standing on chariots, and elephant-riders elephant-riders. / Chariots [struck] chariots, elephants elephants, and horses horses; / heroes on foot [struck] riders, and foot-soldiers female riders.
The goddesses too, greatly enraged in battle, struck down the infantry, / riders, chariots, and elephants of the Danava lords with darts, spears, and axes.
And throwing the heroic Danavas to the ground, they crushed them with their feet; / some shattered the heads of the haters of the gods with their fists.

Tearing open the chests of the haughty [demons] in battle, / some goddesses drank the blood together with the life-breaths of the haters of the gods. / And some, rising up swiftly [though] their weapons were cut to pieces, / enraged, struck the deities with fists clenched like thunderbolts.
Some elephants, whose temple-regions were dark with the flow of rut-fluid, / becoming exceedingly furious, crushed the chariots of the deities in battle.
With swarms of intoxicated six-legged bees clinging to their cheek-walls, / some elephants, whose mahouts had been slain, struck down both Daityas and deities.

7.7.m:
With the sounds of musical instruments, the clashing of bowstrings against armguards, the roars of elephants and horses, and the rumblings of chariot rims, / that entire Vindhya mountain, its hollows and caves completely filled, shook as it were then. / The goddesses, driving back the forces of the enemies in battle, roared loudly with force, / and the Daitya warriors, repelling the goddesses in battle, rejoiced in heart and bellowed.
Sprinkled slightly with blood, the armies surged back and forth there, / like great forests stirred by the wind, with sprouts springing forth. / The severed faces of the vanguard, bright with wondrous golden ornaments, / having fallen in battle by the goddesses, shone like lotuses whose stalks have been cut.
Repelled, with their frightened elephants fleeing and their horse-warriors slain by the deities, / that army wavered as it were, turned back by the lion-like Daitya lords. / Resembling mountains of collyrium, equipped with wondrous bells, / the lordly elephants of the haters of the gods, pierced in their vital spots by excellent arrows by the deities, fell roaring in battle.

7.7.m:
Rushing forward with force and violently struck in battle, their forces quickly fell back, / just like the waters of rivers thrown back upon reaching the great ocean at the time of flood tide. // 8.65.20
And the goddesses and the daityas shone in the great throng, their arrows locked with one another, / like clusters of stars in a cloud when the sun's rays have dimmed.
Then the leaders of the dānavas, standing on their chariots, shouting their names, quickly went out from their own army, / enraged, well-prepared, the foremost of charioteers, bending their wondrous bows.
The goddesses too, even better prepared, standing on chariots, then rushed forward in fury with speed: / Ṣaṣṭhī advanced against Meghasvana, and Mṛtyu, her anger aroused, against Kārtasvara.

Then the goddesses likewise discharged endless arrows—sharp, well-feathered, piercing vital points, / flying far, and with excellent fletching—against the advancing dānava commanders.
Those various splendid arrows, shot back and forth, clashing together, shone / like the mingled rays of the moon and the sun on a cloudless full-moon day at twilight.
The arms of the daitya lords, severed along with their weapons, fell down in battle, struck by the deities, / like great, thick serpent lords with their coils cast off and their tongues swallowed back.
Then in that battle, the enraged Ṣaṣṭhī discharged floods of arrows at Meghasvana; / as they approached from all sides, the daitya cut them down by hundreds in the sky with his arrows.
Then, seeing those arrows severed, she quickly discharged other, lighter shafts;
and the daitya repeatedly sliced those incoming arrows with volleys of shafts.

Pierced by them, his body smeared with blood, utterly confounded, he hung his head somewhat. / His charioteer took him away from the battlefield in his chariot adorned with Jambū river gold.
Kārtasvana released arrows with variegated golden feathers at the goddess in battle; / Mṛtyu, with noble-feathered arrows, severed them with volleys of shafts before they even arrived.

And Mṛtyu quickly killed his horses with separate gold-fletched arrows; / then the daitya leapt down from the chariot whose horses were slain, took up a shield and an excellent polished sword,
enraged, his eyes wide and blood-red, he rushed with speed toward the goddess; / as he charged, Mṛtyu sliced that shield into hundreds of pieces with volleys of sharp-pointed arrows.
With his shield-guard shattered, the asura chief raised his sharp-edged sword / and rushed at Mṛtyu, like a flashing cloud charging Rohiṇī in the sky.
As he charged in battle like Death itself, Mṛtyu struck him with arrows resembling fierce serpents / in his vital parts, which she had targeted, and swiftly parted him from his life.
The invincible Lakṣmī covered Druma, who moved with the grace of an elephant king, with choice arrows, / sharp, straight-flying, shot from the ear, with beautiful gold feathers, in the arena of battle.

Those various, straight-flying, well-fletched shafts fell upon Druma's limbs in battle; / stuck with those wondrous shafts, he shone like a great tree visited by flocks of birds.
Then that king of the Kiṃpuruṣas, steadfast, pierced Lakṣmī with ten well-feathered arrows / in her face that resembled the full moon, and each of her two arms with a hundred and eight.
Paying no heed to those excellent arrows, she of lovely face drove sharp arrows into his face, / and countless other well-fletched ones, tipped with polished gold, individually into his body.
Then the lord of the daityas sliced off the tip of the flagstaff on Lakṣmī's chariot with a sharp broad-headed arrow, / and swiftly pierced her four horses with four [shafts] and her charioteer with an arrow.
Taking an iron shaft, Lakṣmī then struck down the charioteer of the gods' enemy in battle; / she pierced his steeds with separate arrows and quickly cut down the banner of his chariot.

In drawing, fitting to the string, and releasing, in postures, steps, grip, and sharpening, / those two distinguished themselves above each other in the midst of battle through their skill. / Kānti cut down the arrows dispatched by Maya, and Maya the polished shafts of Kānti; / invulnerable, they found no vulnerability whatsoever in each other there.
Into his horses, charioteer, chariot, and flag, and into all the limbs of his body, / Kānti drove straight-flying arrows with golden shafts into Maya.
And Maya covered Kānti, along with her chariot, / charioteer, and splendid, decorated banner and excellent steeds, / with sharp shafts, as a cloud covers a woodland with downpours of rain. / Then, enraged in battle, Kānti, with a superior feathered iron shaft,
swiftly struck down the enemy's charioteer then, and eight horses with eight arrows.

7.7.m:
His horses and charioteer slain, deprived of his chariot, Maya then took up a sharp-edged sword; / having recognized Kānti's prowess in battle, he abandoned the fight and flew up into the sky. / Saramā pierced Mura, the commander of the troop of Dānavas and Daityas, on the battlefield with sharp arrows; / the Daitya too struck Saramā with straight-flying arrows feathered with vulture and peacock plumes.
Enraged then, the goddess severed his ornate bow with a sharp broad-headed arrow. / Seizing another bow then, he pierced the goddess's four horses; / agitated and vomiting blood, struck by the arrows of the Daitya lord, those horses,
panting, fell to the ground in battle and all together quickly gave up their lives.
Then the enraged goddess Saramā, raising a sword of polished blade / and leaping into the air, struck down the Asura's driver and his enormous horses.

Caṇḍā pierced the rushing Ghana in battle with sharp-pointed arrows fletched with gold; / pierced by them, that Daitya lord shone like a dark raincloud [illumined] by the moon's rays. / Disregarding those shafts, Ghana rushed against Caṇḍā, showering a net of arrows;
as he advanced, Caṇḍā pierced his excellent chariot-horses with well-feathered arrows.
The Daitya also severed the high-raised top of her banner and slew the goddess's horses; / leaving their chariots and descending to the ground, taking up excellent shields and swords, the two resolved [to fight].
They moved in circles in the midst of battle, touching the ground with the tips of their toes, / and [traversed] various paths with light steps, yet neither found any vulnerability in the other.

With leaps, high bounds, and lion-like springs, turnings, mock combats, and raised arms, / swooping strikes, retreats, counter-attacks, / ducking postures, dodges, and head strikes, / Caṇḍā then leaped forward swiftly and quickly severed his neck; / with his head severed, the Daitya instantly fell forward onto his chest upon that battlefield.
His body smeared with blood, fallen lifeless upon the earth, / Ghana shone like a dark raincloud in the sky tinged by the vast form of twilight. / Niyati pierced Khara in the chest with sharp, well-feathered arrows fletched with gold / as he charged head-on in battle, and cut down his banner with a broad-headed shaft.

With his head split open, that Dānava shone upon the ground shedding streams of blood, / like a mountain cleaved at the summit by a thunderbolt, pouring out streams of mineral liquid.
The noble Prabhāvatī struck Dhundhu on the chest / with ten straight-flying, well-feathered, sharp-pointed arrows colored like dense storm clouds.
With sixteen arrows she killed the sixteen horses of the gods' enemy; / having struck down the driver of his chariot with one, she severed his banner with another.
Dhundhu hurled a mace weighing a thousand bhāras, adorned with lovely golden bells; / as it came flying, Prabhāvatī cut into hundreds of pieces that [weapon] hurled by the Daitya chief.
Taking a huge iron club, the Daitya leaped from his vehicle and rushed around / toward the goddess on the battlefield, dark as a mountain of collyrium, like Death bearing his staff.

7.7.m:
As that lord of Dānavas rushed forward in battle, the goddess struck him with well-feathered shafts; / ignoring all the arrows of the goddess, he approached her in fury at the front of the fray.
Swinging the iron club, cast forward like the staff of Yama, that broad-armed one / brought that iron club down upon her chariot, like Indra striking the slope of a mountain with his thunderbolt.
He swiftly crushed that chariot of the goddess along with its horses, charioteer, banner, and golden wheels; / the goddess quickly sprang away from there when that iron bar was hurled by the Asura.
Seeing that she had fled from there, taking up that very same iron club, / the chief of Dānava warriors rushed at her, like a dark raincloud in the sky [charging] the bright moon.
Leaping up, she severed his iron club with razor-headed arrows and other [missiles] discharged from excellent divine weapons; / raising his clenched fist, the Daitya then leaped into the sky again toward her.

The goddess swiftly struck that Dānava in his vital parts with prime arrows that pierce the vitals; / pierced by those well-plumed arrows penetrating his vital organs, that foremost Dānava warrior vanished.
Then, as the battle was abandoned by the chiefs of warriors,
who had departed with their prowess and valor thwarted, / the enemies of the lord of the gods, roaring aloud,
mounted excellent elephants, taking up their weapons.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, named 'The Battle of the Goddesses,' in the war of Śumbha and Niśumbha in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
The goddesses too, discerning their effort, carefully mounted supreme elephants— / pure, dripping rut-fluid, with splendid tusks, with excellent bodies, cloths, and flanks of trunks,
with beautiful trunk-tips, high round frontal globes, fine tails, curved and lovely ears, / good tusk-sheaths, eyes like sparrows, wide chests, and backbones comfortable for sitting,

fit for war, foremost in speed, in the prime of life, well-trained, with elevated forebodies, / with armor, weapons, and diverse bells fastened on them, and lofty banners and flags raised high.
Adorned with banners and pennants, and decorated with diverse multi-colored weapons, / those herds of elephants then appeared like forests colliding into forests in the woods.
The Daityas too, six of them upon the heads of elephants, / twanging their bows, shone resplendent
like clouds settled upon mountains, accompanied by rainbows and filled with the roar of thunderbolts.
Those troops of elephants in the battle, swiftly driven forward by mahouts, / rushed at each other, driven on like masses of clouds by the wind.
Rushing impetuously against elephants, elephants in rut struck those whose faces were dark with temporal fluid, / striking them in the hollows of their temples with tusks bound with iron and white as lotus stalks.

struck by the goddesses in battle, like huge boulders of the lords of the Daityas tossed down by the wind.
Approaching by scent the chief elephants lying lifeless on the battleground like great dark mountains, / some elephants, furious with rut, lowered their heads and trumpeted with their mouths.
Severed faces wearing earrings and arms with weapons smeared with fine sandalwood paste / fell from the elephants of the Asura generals, cut down by the goddesses in battle with sharp razor-headed arrows.
All around, bows hummed loudly; the chiefs of the gods' enemies roared as they struck; / bowstrings twanged when drawn and released; and elephants pierced by arrows sank down.
With elephants falling, pierced by arrows, their handsome backs bearing high-raised large banners, / the earth was covered over as if with the foot of mountains bearing palm trees thrown down by the wind.
Elephants struck elephants in the slaughter, and Daityas [struck] the goddesses, and the goddesses [struck] the sons of Diti; / there the lordly elephants [struck] Daityas, and the Daityas, enraged, rushed against the furious elephants. // 16

Swiftly the horses fell lifeless; the rut-maddened elephants, rut dripping, stumbled; / the best warriors among the enemies of the gods, struck by arrows, all trembled together in battle. // 24
Just as a blazing fire ignited with radiant flames burns dry thickets unobstructed, / so Kauśikī in battle burned the armies of the enemies of the gods with blazing showers of arrows. // 25
Just as the sun at midday makes the shadow of stationary and moving beings small, / so the Goddess in battle reduced that army of the enemies to a tiny remnant. // 26
Then the two lords of the Dānavas, challenging the Goddess and bending their two great bows, rushed forward; / with sharp, well-feathered arrows they covered Kauśikī on the battlefield. // 27
Intent on her bows, her lions, and her banners, the two mighty-armed lords of the Daityas, their minds overwhelmed with anger, / drove excellent, well-feathered arrows into the deity in battle. // 28

She then killed the horses and the two charioteers, severed the two splendid banners of their chariots, / and drove other excellent gold-shafted arrows into the vital spots of the two enemies of the gods. // 32
Abandoning their chariots, Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two lords of the Daityas, afflicted by the excellent arrows, / seized two excellent swords and then leaped into the sky, dark as a sharp blade. // 33
Then in the cloudless sky, dark as polished swords,
advancing very swiftly and seizing by the necks / those two lords of Diti's sons, the Goddess quickly crushed them,
praised by the foremost sages freed from fear and despair. // 34
Vomiting foamy blood from their mouths,
their prowess instantly destroyed, all the joints of their limbs crushed, / their life-breaths departed, their eyes rolled back in red,
the two lion-like Daityas fell down upon the surface of the earth. // 35
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, named 'The Slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha,' in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.7.m:
The seers, O goddess, now offer the purifying oblation; / and they recite the Vedic meters aloud and practice their religious vows. (7)
Sacrifice rich with many priestly gifts is celebrated now by brahmins, / and the sages sleep happily in their leaf-huts, full of trust. (8) / The good who have resorted to the path of virtue sit without fear, O goddess; / the path of righteous deeds, which had been broken off, has appeared again in the world. (9)
Through your grace the world-guardians hold their heads held high, / and a pleasant breeze blows, mingled with the pollen of flowers. (10)
Free from weariness through your grace, O one of great yoga, / the rivers carry clear and cool waters, O goddess. (11) / And now the mountains, O daughter of the Mountain-born, have become / feverless again, bearing streams of cool, sweet cascade-waters. (12)
The hooded serpents hold their hoods high, marked with svastikas and discuses; / and the oceans, confident, now rest peacefully. (13) / Through your grace, O goddess, apsarases now wander / in the sky that is as pure as a virtuous mind, their eyes languid with playfulness. (14)

7.7.m:
Thus addressed by the gods, the goddess said, smiling slightly, as it were: / “I wish to see my father, who wears the crescent moon upon his crest, (19) / well-pleased, and my gracious mother, the daughter of the mountain. / And once permitted by my parents, you may then consecrate me.” (20)
Thus addressed, the gods with attentive minds then meditated / upon Mahādeva, attended by his consort, of immeasurable splendor and prowess. (21)
Then the gods beheld the god of gods, the lord of Umā, / standing before them like an accumulation of all radiances, (22)
Bearing upon his head a lofty mass of matted locks, tawny at their edges, / like a blazing fire of radiant flames, (23)
Bathed in holy ash white like camphor flakes, / like a lofty silver mountain draped with a network of golden creepers at its edge, (24)
Obscuring with his own radiance the radiances of the celestials, / as the sun at midday obscures the flames of lamps, (25)

Wearing a lion skin, uneven, lustrous, heavy, / grey with ashes of powder, hanging down, slightly folded; (27) / having a great lord of serpents gliding over his chest, / its body bathed at the edges by the rays of the jewels of its hoods; (28)
And [beholding] Bhavānī standing at his side, blazing with her own splendor, / wearing a red garment born of the wish-fulfilling tree, (29)
Wearing upon her head a blossoming garland of mandāra flowers / frequented by swarms of intoxicated bees, tawny with the heap of its pollen, (30)
Adorned with excellent ornaments fashioned by the craftsman of heaven, wondrous, / surrounded by rays of gems, made of gold, and praiseworthy, (31)
Wearing around her neck a splendid, pure, peerless single-strand necklace / of medium size, spotless as the autumn moonbeams. (32)
Then all the gods arose, and Kauśikī, bowing their faces, / fell at the lotus feet of the two, their minds rejoicing. (33) / Then Mahādeva, looking up at Kauśikī, said this: / “Unconquerable by all beings, endowed with great yoga, of great splendor, (34)

"And just as the gods, yakṣas, great serpents, / gandharvas, sages, and siddhas worship me, so also, O blameless one, / devotees will worship you everywhere and praise you, O imperishable one!" / Having thus given the boon to her, the daughter of the mountain and the bull-bannered [Śiva],

"Let the earth be swiftly adorned completely with heaps of various flowers! / Fragrant with the flower-pollen of shrubs, bushes, creepers, and trees, / captivating the minds here, let pleasant breezes blow! / Let the clouds sprinkle the plateau of the Vindhya with holy waters!

her limbs adorned with pearl garlands, wearing white garlands and unguent, / then the seven seers, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Yajña, Prajāpati,
the Ādityas, Kaśyapa, the Rudras, the world-protectors, the sacrificial fires, / the lords of mountains, the Earth, Gaṅgā, the Moon, the Maruts, the two Aśvins, / the oceans, the Vasus, Lakṣmī, Sandhyā, Kīrti, Sarasvatī, / the serpent lords, the lords of birds, and various excellent rivers,
taking all the water jars, consecrated Kauśikī. / Resembling the orb of the full moon, with a gem-encrusted staff and great splendor,
Śatakratu himself held the wide umbrella. / And with long flywhisks with golden handles, spotless like moonbeams,
the world-protectors then fanned the imperishable one with effort. / And then the glorious Pākaśāsana [Indra] said to Kauśikī:

सनत्कुमार उवाच
7.7.m:
"Protect the entire earth, O goddess; you are my sister, O imperishable one! / Bestow favor upon your devotees, O sovereign lady, and slay the thorns of the immortals! / Roam through all the worlds, worshipped by the hosts of siddhas!"
Having spoken these words to Kauśikī, the king of gods,
accompanied by the host of deities, wearing a large, bright, dangling necklace, / then flew up from the Vindhya, scattering in the sky blue
clouds heavy with water and bowed down on all sides.
Whoever hears this always, or reads it in an assembly of the virtuous, / having attained happiness in this world, goes to the supreme state.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, named The Consecration of Kauśikī, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Then the illustrious goddess Kauśikī established those deities / born from her body in the regions and cities.

Grasping that enemy of Indra by the tail, forcefully placing her foot upon his head, / taking up her trident, she pierced his back and quickly separated the daitya from his life-breaths. // 23 // / [Apparatus readings]

Vyāsa said:
O blessed one, knower of all the worlds, having splendour equal to the Grandfather, / having performed plentiful austerity at that time, the daughter of the Himavat, // 1 // / having obtained the desired boon of fair complexion from Brahmā— / what else did she do at the end of her austerity, O great sage, O brahmin? // 2
And what auspicious boon did Somanandin the tiger obtain? / Tell this to me as I ask, for I am devoted and bowed in reverence. // 3 // / Sanatkumāra said:

Then, seeing the devoted Nandīśvara with affection, the daughter of the king of mountains / said to him at that time: 'Come, child! You are seen after a long time.' // 10
And seeing her, fair-limbed and shining like gold, / filled with great joy, Nandī fell prostrate at her feet.
Having bowed down, the wise one then praised the mountain's daughter: / 'Salutations to Siddhi, to the Great Goddess, to Rati, to Gati, salutations!
You are ritual action, you are the cause, and you are material nature and liberation itself; / [you are] loveliness, radiance, and contentment, peace, [and] the supreme source of welfare.
[You are] the sacrificial fee, cosmic order, death, twilight, lightning, day, and night; / [you are] the earth, Kauśikī, and Śrī, Śarvāṇī, the beloved of Śarva,
mother of the gaṇas, and Diti, the pure Vindhyavāsinī, / Kṛṣṇā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, mother of living beings, and the Sovereign Lady.
O Goddess, be gracious to me, your devotee, who has bowed down.' / Then the Goddess, seeing Nandī bowed down at her feet,

'How fortunate you are with a delighted face! How fortunate that your austerity has borne fruit! / How fortunate [you are with] this excellent fair complexion, shining like gold! / It is exceedingly dear to us, O Goddess, that you have returned in every way, / having fulfilled your vow here. And whence is this tiger of yours?'
Being addressed thus by her husband with gentle affection, the Goddess / told the God all her adventures. / The Goddess said:
'When previously, O God, you addressed me as "dark-complexioned," / then, my limbs filled with anger, longing for a fair complexion, / I went to a peak of the Himālaya and undertook great austerity. / Always meditating upon you, I stood upon one foot.
On the very day that I took refuge in austerity there, / on that very day this tiger, Somanandī, stood before me,
O Mahādeva, endowed with supreme devotion. / Engaged in that austerity, I remained for a divine thousand years.
For that entire time, he too remained near me, / gazing with tail, eyes, and mouth held motionless, fasting.

7.7.m:
'In that region where, O Mahādeva, the excellent austerity was performed, / that [place] I desire to see once more together with you, O Śaṅkara.' / Sanatkumāra said:
Being addressed thus by Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord replied: / 'O fair-limbed one, O imperishable lady, it pleases me also to go there.
Charming is that Himālayan peak where the austerity was performed by you.' / Then, having summoned Nandī and the leaders of the gaṇas by the thousands, / he set out together with the Goddess to the Himālaya, the great mountain, / accompanied by gods, vidyādharas, siddhas, gandharvas, and the foremost sages,
the God being repeatedly saluted and praised on all sides. / Mounted upon Nandī's back, the lord of the gaṇas disported himself.
Having arrived at the Himālaya mountain, he came to that region. / Reaching that charming peak adorned with mineral ores,
the Lord of Gaṇas was supremely delighted and took pleasure [there]. / Then, seeing that he had arrived, the mountain in embodied form / approached Mahādeva, bowed down with joined palms.

Whoever, having observed a pure vow, stays for three nights, climbs you, / beholds Gaurī, and, having worshipped [her], satisfies a brahmin...'
whether a woman or a man, that person shall go to Gaurī’s world. / And whoever abandons their life-breaths here, concentrated in religious observance, // having attained the status of a gaṇa-leader, shall wander together with me. / And Gaurī’s presence will always remain right here for you.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to that best of mountains, the god of gods, the three-eyed one, / accompanied by Pārvatī, walked all around there.
Then, O Vyāsa, he saw a golden stone adorned with jewels; / that Lord said to the Goddess: “Behold that stone!”
The Goddess said to him, the Lord of Gods: “Austerity was performed by me here; / thus this place is dear to me and to Somanandin.”

Then, while strolling, the divine Lord asked Pārvatī again: / “How did these pools come to be here, O mountain-born lady?” // Being thus questioned, the Goddess spoke this speech again: / “When I came here to perform austerity, O divine Lord,
then two great streams repeatedly flowed from my breasts; / by those two, these two pools were made, containing white water and great abundance.
When I cast off my ornaments in order to perform austerity, / then from them, O Lord, a flowing stream of water fell swiftly;
and in this way, this second auspicious pool of water was made by me. / And when the supreme fair-complexioned state was obtained from Brahmā,
then, O Lord, a dark sheath emerged from my body; / out of that sheath, this third pool was produced.
In this region, O Lord of Gods, having duly worshipped you, / fire rites were performed by me with oblations accompanied by mantras.

7.7.m:
Whoever satiates the ancestors, his śrāddha shall be inexhaustible; / and whoever gives a brown cow here to a brahmin with concentration, // he will obtain the fruit of a thousand cows, O fair-faced one. / Because having mounted the summit you performed austerity here,
this will be known everywhere by the name Agrāraṇya, / yielding great fruit, greatly sacred, granting all perfections, auspicious, // the excellent peak of Gaurī, extending for five yojanas.
Having fasted here, pure, having bathed, endowed with supreme devotion—
having reached the end of their bodily existence, shines mounted upon an aerial chariot. / Highly meritorious is your black antelope skin, which removes all sin. / The brahmin who beholds this—heaven is not hard for him to attain; / whatever fruit is gained in Naimiṣāraṇya, and whatever fruit at Puṣkara,
that very fruit does the twice-born obtain, O goddess, upon seeing the black antelope skin. / And I shall dwell here continually together with you, my beloved.

7.7.m:
O goddess, whatever man worships us two residing here, / he will become a leader of our gaṇas and traverse the entire world. / Having thus shown favor to the king of mountains at that time together with the mountain-king's daughter, O best of sages, / Śarva, followed by gods and siddhas, returned once more to Mandara.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, entitled "The Bestowal of Boons at the Kośī Stone, the Breast-Pool, the Antelope Skin, and the Gaurī Peak," in the reunion with the goddess in the Skandapurāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Having gone back to Mandara together with the mountain's daughter, what did the Lord, / Mahādeva, do? Tell me that, O great sage.

7.7.m:
Having arrived at Mount Mandara together with Pārvatī, Hara / took delight in that golden, divine [realm] adorned with all kinds of jewels,
furnished with lovely stairways and multicolored marble flagstones, / in that excellent, foremost city fashioned at that time by his mind,
served by the lords of gaṇas endowed with great yoga, led by Nandīśvara, / and by siddhas and the best of sages, the Lord of the world
dwelt together with the goddess, and likewise praised [by all]. / While that wise God of gods was sporting in this way, O Vyāsa,
the thousand-eyed one, the moon, and Vāyu then departed. / Approaching the city gate and seeing Nandin stationed [there],
desiring to behold Śaṅkara, they with folded hands said: / "O Nandin, you ought to arrange that we may see the Lord of gods." / Then Nandī, having gone and stood at the base of the doorway, / announced to Śambhu the three gods who had arrived.
When Nandin was commanded by the God of gods, "Let them enter," / those three gods then entered into the presence of Śaṅkara.

7.7.m:
Hiraṇyakaśipu the elder and Hiraṇyākṣa the younger. / Formerly consecrated by Brahmā, he had become the king of the daityas.
Then the mighty Vipracitti was in the sovereign status of the dānavas, / and the thousand-eyed one in that of the gods; thus this triad of Indras shone forth. / Then while they were ruling the three worlds, O Vyāsa, / the daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, wishing to seize the realm of Śakra
in order to bring the three worlds under his own control, set his mind on austerity. / Going to the southern quarter and settling upon Śrīparvata,
the mighty king of the daityas performed intense, severe austerity. / He offered oblations into the fire of sacrificial firewood and caru mixed with his own blood.
With raised arms, without support, gazing at the sun by day, / standing on one foot without blinking, he remained resolute. // 31
The mighty one stood thus for two thousand divine years. / By his immense austerity, the three worlds were agitated. // 32 // / Then Brahmā, the foremost of the gods, who rides upon a lotus, approached / and respectfully said to him, 'O king, choose a desired boon.' // 33

Then Hiraṇyakaśipu, the foremost of all asuras, / having conquered Indra, the son of Diti himself ruled the kingdom. // 39
Appropriating the three worlds to himself and conquering all the celestials, / he himself became Indra, himself Vāyu, himself Yama; / he himself became Kubera, Varuṇa, and Agni—he became everything himself. // 40
'Bow down to me! Sacrifice to me! I am Brahmā along with Indra!' / Thus that asura spoke to all the seers, siddhas, and brahmins. // 41
Vyāsa said:
This mountain that was called Śrīparvata by you, O best of sages: / why is it called Śrīparvata? What is the merit there, and what is the fruit? // 42
Sanatkumāra said:
Lo, I shall tell you what you ask me, O you of noble vows, / where the daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed great austerity. // 43
On that very sacred mountain, the God of gods, who has the bull as his banner, / accompanied by goddess Umā, sported constantly, endowed with great splendor. // 44
As the god remained there, the goddess, the daughter of the best of mountains, / [saw] those perfected through austerity, great yogins possessing the radiance of blazing suns. // 45

7.7.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
While that Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was ruling then,
a great length of time passed, O Vyāsa, over the three worlds with their moving and unmoving beings. / 1
Possessed by immense arrogance, his mind deranged by pride in his prosperity,
he disdained all the gods and did not observe dharma. / 2
Infuriated with anger, he brought severe affliction
upon all the gods together, Śakra and the others, though banished from their own realm. / 3
Being tormented, they all went to Brahmā for refuge:
"O Lord, master of what was and is to be, grandfather, of great splendour! / 4
O sinless one, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, having obtained a boon from you,
has overrun all three worlds and seized our heavenly kingdom. / 5
And he constantly heaps humiliation upon us, inflicting the torment of enmity.
Routed by him, we have all come to you for refuge. / 6
Grant your grace, O lord of the gods, so that he may no longer be our enemy—
the powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu, who has abandoned dharma and become the foe of the world." / 7
Thus addressed then by the gods, the god whose vehicle is the lotus,
endowed with great wisdom, spoke this word bringing joy to the gods: / 8

7.7.m:
"O Lord, from Hiraṇyakaśipu, the exceedingly powerful king of the Daityas,
great fear has arisen for us, and our kingdom in heaven has been seized. / 19
Humiliation has also been inflicted on us by him, O best of the gods.
He enjoys the entire world—that hater of Brahmā, son of Kaśyapa! / 20

O slayer of all enemies, act in such a way that this Daitya is killed by you;
make it so, O Hṛṣīkeśa! Let this boon be granted to us." / 21

7.7.m:
Then Viṣṇu, having meditated for a long time and reflected on the means of killing him,
spoke to the gods, the best of the deities, as if invigorating them with his word: / 22
"So be it, O best of gods! I will carry out all your words.
Since he is a king of Daityas of great strength, I tell you: / 23
Enter my body too, O you of virtuous vows!
Embodying all the gods, I shall slay your arrogant enemy." / 24
Then all the gods entered the body of Viṣṇu.
And he, becoming mighty and assuming a terrifying form, / 25
the man-lion of great splendour, adorned with claws and fangs,
Viṣṇu went, shining forth, to the city of Hiraṇyakaśipu. / 26
Having seen outside his garden, filled with flowers of all seasons,
the man-lion stood greatly astonished at [the garden of] the lion of the Daityas. / 27
It was adorned on all sides with campaka, aśoka, and jātī trees,
with kadambas and bakulas, and with fragrant flowers, / 28

with lakes covered with lotuses and adorned by swans and cakravāka birds,
and with trees bearing desired fruits—a forest resembling the celestial Vaibhrāja. / 29
Moving playfully, high with fury, the man-lion shattered it;
he agitated the lakes like an elephant fierce with rut. / 30
Standing in the midst of the forest, roaming here and there, he shone
like a loftily raised peak of Meru, the king of mountains. / 31
Then, approaching that man-lion, the forest-guards, filled with rage—
powerful though they were—sought to restrain him; and the mighty one struck them down. / 32
